questions.q: What is the main purpose of this lesson's review checklist, per the lesson's own framing?
options: To turn the concepts already covered across Chapters 1 through 3 into a single, repeatable checklist an architect actually uses when reviewing a proposed integration design
To introduce entirely new integration concepts not covered elsewhere in the course
To replace the need for understanding idempotency or retry strategy
To serve only as exam trivia with no practical review application
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states its job is synthesis: consolidating pattern fit, limits, failure semantics, security, monitoring, and governance concepts already taught into one practical, repeatable review checklist.

questions.q: In the worked review example, why does the proposed synchronous Apex trigger logging to an analytics platform fail the "pattern fit" checklist item?
options: Because synchronous callouts are always forbidden under any circumstances
Because Apex triggers cannot make callouts of any kind
Because logging an analytics event has no business reason to block the Opportunity-saving transaction — it should be fire-and-forget rather than a synchronous callout
Because analytics platforms never accept API calls from Salesforce
questions.explain: The core pattern-fit question is whether the business process genuinely needs to wait for an answer. Logging an event has no such need, so coupling the Opportunity save to a synchronous callout is a pattern-fit failure — this should be fire-and-forget instead.

questions.q: Why does the worked example's design fail the "failure semantics" checklist item?
options: Because it uses a Named Credential instead of hard-coded credentials
Because there is no retry strategy and no idempotency consideration, so a transient failure could either silently drop the log entry or, if retried naively, double-log it
Because the integration runs too infrequently to matter
Because Apex triggers cannot access external analytics platforms
questions.explain: With no retry logic and no idempotency plan, the design has no defined behavior for a transient failure — it could silently lose data or, if a naive retry were later added, create duplicate log entries, exactly the gap the failure-semantics checklist item is meant to catch.

questions.q: Why does hard-coding API credentials directly in the Apex class fail the review checklist's security item?
options: Hard-coded credentials actually pass this checklist item without issue
Because hard-coded credentials are always encrypted automatically by the platform
Because Apex classes cannot technically store any credential value
Because credentials embedded in code can't be rotated or updated without a code deployment, unlike credentials managed through a Named Credential
questions.explain: A Named Credential centralizes where authentication details live so they can be rotated in one place; hard-coding credentials in Apex means any credential change requires a full code deployment, which the security checklist item specifically flags as a problem.

questions.q: What does this lesson argue is the core reason a review checklist should be run during the architecture phase rather than after an integration has already shipped?
options: Because every problem the checklist catches is far cheaper to fix on a whiteboard than after the integration is live and a production incident forces an emergency redesign under pressure
Because reviews are only legally required before deployment, not after
Because a checklist run after shipping is always inaccurate
Because post-incident reviews are explicitly banned by this course's governance model
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument, echoing Lesson 11, is that fixing a flawed design before implementation is dramatically cheaper than fixing it after go-live, under the pressure of an active production incident.
